summary: When you sell a Connecticut one- or two-family home or a condo-type unit, you must hand the buyer a signed affidavit at closing saying the home has working smoke detection and either working CO detection or no CO risk at all.
alarmType: Smoke detection equipment must be installed in or immediately near each bedroom and must sound an audible alarm when you press the test button. The statute does not itself require hardwiring, interconnection, sealed 10-year batteries or photoelectric sensing; it only requires the affidavit to disclose, to the seller's best knowledge, whether the equipment is battery powered, where it sits relative to bedrooms, whether it runs on household electrical service, and whether it is interconnected. For a building built before January 1, 1990 the seller may state that the interconnection item does not apply.
coAlarms: Handled in the same affidavit. The seller states either that the CO detection equipment complies, or that the property poses no CO risk because it has no fuel-burning appliance, fireplace or attached garage. CO equipment may be battery operated and must sound an audible alarm when the test button is pressed.
certification: The seller self-certifies. No inspection, fire marshal certificate or third-party sign-off is required; the transferor signs and dates the affidavit and presents it to the buyer at closing. The affidavit creates no warranty beyond transfer of title. The Office of the State Fire Marshal must publish a model affidavit form, developed with a realtors' association, a bar association and a fire marshals' association, plus a guide to help sellers fill it in. The section states no fine or buyer credit for failing to give the affidavit.
citation: Conn. Gen. Stat. 29-453 (smoke and carbon monoxide detectors required in certain residential buildings)
lastAmended: 2023 (P.A. 23-164, effective October 1, 2023; section originally enacted by P.A. 13-272 effective January 1, 2014, then amended by P.A. 14-219 and P.A. 22-75)
notVerified: The current (2025/2026 revision) statute text. The Connecticut General Assembly site could not be fetched by curl at all: every request to cga.ct.gov failed TLS verification ("unable to get local issuer certificate") across default, --cacert and --capath settings and with HTTP/1.1 and TLS 1.2 forced. The current-revision page https://www.cga.ct.gov/current/pub/chap_541a.htm and the Office of Legislative Research report https://cga.ct.gov/2024/rpt/pdf/2024-R-0133.pdf were both blocked by robots. The text used here is the 2024 General Statutes supplement page for chapter 541a plus the official text of P.A. 23-164; a search found no public act amending 29-453 after 2023, but 2024-2026 sessions were not exhaustively checked.
Exact statutory wording was summarized by a page reader rather than read verbatim, so subdivision lettering and precise phrasing should be re-checked against the official text before publication.

Exempt transfers were listed from the 2024 supplement page: transfers between co-owners; gratuitous transfers to a spouse, parent, sibling, child, grandparent or grandchild; court-ordered transfers; transfers by the federal government or its political subdivisions; deeds in lieu of foreclosure; transfers incident to refinancing existing mortgage debt; mortgage deeds or instruments securing debt where title is subject to a preexisting mortgage; transfers by executors, administrators, trustees or conservators; and property acquired by strict foreclosure or foreclosure by sale. This list was not confirmed against verbatim statute text.
Whether any separate Connecticut statute or the State Building Code imposes a smoke or CO alarm requirement independent of the sale affidavit was not researched.
